reason: Gemmae can be spherical. Some examples ('spherical clusters') describe the clusters, not the gemmae.
Decurrent describes a leaf base running down the stem. The examples are moss leaves, so the pair comes from a wrong part reading, not from an awn.
Laesura present or absent is a normal spore character. The examples with measurements are about its length.
Winged legumes are normal, for example Pterocarpus and Dalbergia.
Fused (connate) cotyledons are a real character.
A palate (corolla throat swelling) can be prominent. The examples are correct.
A fig ostiole can be sunken. One French example may refer to another part.
Aril thickness is meaningful. Thickness is mapped to depth here. If PATO has a separate thickness term, a rule should move 'thick' there.
Scattered nodules on roots is a valid distribution. One example ('in the blade') is not about nodules.
Dot-like (punctiform) nodules is a valid description of nodule shape.

The examples mix arrangement of cymes within the plant (solitary, paired, clustered) with cyme shape (capitate). A rule would need to separate the cyme itself from the arrangement of cymes, and use a value term, not the attribute.
Ploidy of the plant is meaningful. The examples are correct, including chromosome counts.
A sepal outer surface can be silky or sericeous.
Areole width is a real measurement in cacti.
An obconic anther is rare but real. The examples are consistent.
The petal surface can be papillose, which is a texture. A specific papillose value would be better than the attribute.
Optical quality is the wrong reading of a colour description. The examples are 'dark to pale brown' for achenes, which are fruits. Colour has its own pair.
Shallow leaf sinuses are standard.
Wool colour in an areole is meaningful. The wool is not named as its own part.
The examples describe filiform axes inside the inflorescence (rachis, branches, peduncles, scapes), not the inflorescence itself. A rule would need to choose the named sub-part as the bearer.
Pappus scales can have an entire margin. The examples are correct.
Stem height (tall) is meaningful.
'Angled' means angular in cross section, not bent. The PATO synonym gives a wrong reading. Use an angular or ridged shape term.
A serrate costa is common in mosses.
Tapering involucral bracts are normal.
Hispidulous leaflets are normal.
A sinuous lamina or lamina margin is a valid character. Flexuous and sinuous mean roughly the same here.
Presence of a seta (for example on teeth) is a valid statement. Some examples describe seta shape, which should get its own quality.
An operculum present or absent is a standard character. 'Anther operculate' belongs to another part.
Fruits can be opaque. The examples are correct.
Elongated stolons are meaningful.
A floccose pedicel is meaningful.
Valves can be exserted, for example in capsules.
Glands (secretory tissue) can be elongated. The bearer is vague but the examples are about glands.
A pale involucral bract is a colour statement. Low saturation is a loose reading, but it is acceptable.
Corona lobes can be oblong. Some examples are corona scales or arms, which are other parts.
Veins hidden or concealed is a standard leaf character. The bearer is the vascular bundle (veins).
A tapered thorn is normal. Some examples ('base tapering') describe other parts.
A papery or chartaceous endocarp is meaningful.
Perichaetia present or numerous is a valid moss character. Position examples ('on terminal branches') are a different quality.
Chestnut or castaneous is a red-brown colour. Some examples refer to costae and stalks.
Short involucral bracts are meaningful. Some examples are about the petaloid portions.
Filament orientation (spreading, parallel) is meaningful.
Pappus parts can be irregular. Some examples are about scale margins or length.

The examples (truncate margins, funnelform, obtuse apex) are not about an ochrea but about other organs. A rule would need to require the ochrea to be named, and a value term instead of the shape attribute.
Narrow pappus bristles or scales are meaningful.
A labellum lobe can be orbicular. Some examples are a callus or a different lobe.
A tree crown can be flattened. The examples ('cime', 'dôme aplati') actually describe a cyme, so the bearer is wrong for some rows.
A corolla lip can be spatulate.
Length of perichaetal bracts is meaningful.
Dimorphic is a value, not the attribute morphology. A rule would need to map 'dimorphic' to a specific value term and keep the attribute only for plain statements.
Pyrenes can be flattened. The examples fit.
A woolly (lanate) stamen or filament is meaningful.
The examples are 'capillary' (hair-thin), which is a shape, not fibrillary (made of small fibres).
Petals can be inrolled. This is a rolled margin and fits the introverted reading.
Terete prickles are meaningful.
Leathery or coriaceous bracts are meaningful.
A sericeous style is meaningful.
A velvety or velutinous corolla is meaningful.
A tubular ochrea is a standard character in Polygonaceae.
